title: Single personal pronouns and nominal phrase

blocks.text: The Italian says "I'm a cop." Arabic says "Cops": . ⁧أَنَا شُرْطِيٌّ⁩ At present there is no verb "to be" and the phrase is based on two names placed next to each other. It is the nominal phrase, the most frequent structure of written Arabic. In this unity learn the singular pronouns and words to present yourself and others: who they are, what work they do, where they come from.

rows: 6–7 hours · one week (week 14 of the calendar)

blocks.text: Materials This unit, Anki deck A1 (tag A1-02), script for speech synthesis, session with tutor
Targets. At the end of the lesson you know:
1. use the five singular pronouns ⁧أَنَا، أَنْتَ، أَنْتِ، هُوَ، هِيَ⁩ ;
2. build nominal sentences to the present without verb "to be" ;
3. tell your work and that of other people, male and female;
4. tell where you come from with ⁧مِنْ⁩ , even before the article ( ⁧مِنَ القَاهِرَةِ⁩ );
5. understand short presentations read or heard and present three people.
Plan of the week.

I'm Maria. I'm an engineer from Rome.
⁧أَنَا طَبِيبٌ⁩ . ⁧أَنَا أَحْمَد⁩ : ⁧أَحْمَد⁩ ⁧مِنْ سُورِيَا، وَأَنَا طَالِبٌ هُنَا⁩ . ⁧أَيْضًا⁩

blocks.text: What to notice. No bar contains ... are... ⁧أَنَا شُرْطِيٌّ⁩ It's a complete sentence. Ahmad was born in Syria but grew up in Italy: he speaks the family dialect and attends the course to learn Arabic standard, a frequent situation among Arabic speakers of the second generation. Salmā addresses him with ⁧أَنْتَ⁩ even if we would use the standard Arabic in English: it does not have a pronoun of courtesy; respect is expressed by the title ( ⁧يَا أُسْتَاذُ⁩ ) and with formulas.

rows: Man or woman. The final alif is written but in the speech the a is often short: [ʔana]
It's written as ⁧أَنْتِ⁩ : only the final vowel distinguishes them
In texts without vowels decides the context

blocks.text: ⁧هِيَ⁩ Hiya her; it also for things of female gender

Because gender is important. In Arabic, every name is male or female, and the pronouns "he/she" also apply to things: ⁧الكِتَابُ؟ هُوَ هُنَا⁩ Is it the book? It is (Lett. It) here. You'll see better in A1-03. The final vowels of the pronouns never fall. The pause rule (A1-01Section 0) is about desinences, not pronouns: it always says door, anti, huwa, hiya, even at the end of sentence. In texts without vowels ⁧أنت⁩ it can be anta or anti: it is decided who is the person you are talking about.

A nominal sentence has two parts: the subject (in Arabic ⁧مُبْتَدَأ⁩ mubtadaʾ , "what you begin with") and the predicate ( ⁧خَبَر⁩ ḫabar , • information •). At present there is no verb between the two parts.

⁧هُوَ⁩ ⁧مِنْ سُورِيَا⁩ He's from Syria How it works. Arabic considers the link between subject and predicate to the present evident, and does not express it. The verb "to be" appears only when it is necessary to indicate a different time (past, future: A2) or in particular constructions. For this reason, do not insert anything between the subject and the predicate: ⁧أَنَا هُوَ طَالِبٌ⁩ It's wrong. The deal. The predicate agrees in general with the subject: ⁧هُوَ طَالِبٌ⁩ , ⁧هِيَ طَالِبَةٌ⁩ . The feminine of almost all professional names is formed by ⁧ة⁩ . Use it in this unit; in A1-03 You'll see the rules and exceptions. The predicate does not have the article. In ⁧أَنَا طَالِبٌ⁩ "I'm a student" is the predicate indeterminate: ⁧الـ⁩ and with the tanwīn (-one), which corresponds to our . Arabic does not have a word for "un" .

rows: I'm a cop (I say my job).
I'm the cop (the one we talk about).
You are the teacher (of the course).

blocks.text: The article identifies a person already known (I am the one there); without article describes it . In modules and presentations, indeterminate predicate is almost always used.

⁧مِنْ⁩ min .'da, followed by the name of a country or city, indicates where: ⁧أَنَا مِنْ إِيطَالِيَا⁩ anā min Īṭāliyā I'm Italian, I'm from Italy. Before the Article ⁧مِنْ⁩ Take vowel to: ⁧مِنَ القَاهِرَةِ⁩ mina l-Qāhira From Cairo ⁧مِنَ المَغْرِبِ⁩ mina l-Maġrib From Morocco. It's the vowel of support you know from ⁧عَنِ التَّحْقِيقِ⁩ , but for ⁧مِنْ⁩ It's always in. Names of countries with the article. Some countries have the article in the name: ⁧القَاهِرَة⁩ (Cairo), ⁧المَغْرِب⁩ (Morocco), ⁧العِرَاق⁩ (Iraq), ⁧السُّودَان⁩ (Sudan). Other not: ⁧مِصْر⁩ (Egypt), ⁧سُورِيَا⁩ (Syria), ⁧لُبْنَان⁩ (Lebanon), ⁧تُونِس⁩ (Tunisia, Tunis), ⁧إِيطَالِيَا⁩ , ⁧رُومَا⁩ , ⁧مِيلَانُو⁩ . You learn them as whole words; in A1-07 You will pass from Egypt to Egyptian. The proper names are printed without the final vowel of the case ( ⁧يُوسُف⁩ , ⁧أَحْمَد⁩ , ⁧كَرِيم⁩ ), as they usually read; in the vocation with ⁧يَا⁩ take -u: . ⁧يَا كَرِيمُ⁩

blocks.text: . ⁧هُوَ لُوكَا، هُوَ شُرْطِيٌّ أَيْضًا⁩ : ⁧كَرِيم⁩ Karīm: huwa Lūkā, huwa šurṭiyyun ayḍan. Karīm: This is Luca, he's a cop too. . ⁧لُوكَا صَدِيقِي⁩ Lūkā ṣadīqī. Luca's my friend. What to notice. ⁧صَدِيقِي⁩ ṣadīqī My friend uses the suffix -ī of ⁧اِسْمِي⁩ . For a friend: ⁧صَدِيقَتِي⁩ ṣadīqatī , ⁧ة⁩ which becomes ⁧ت⁩ before the suffix (L0-10). In ⁧شُرْطِيَّةٌ جَدِيدَةٌ⁩ the adjective follows the name and takes the female: you will study it in A1-03.

The ⁧هُوَ⁩ and ⁧هِيَ⁩ . Italians tend not to pronounce it: uwa, iya. ⁧ه⁩ It is a consonant: a light but audible breath [h]. Do not confuse it with ⁧ح⁩ of ⁧حَال⁩ , more tense and without vibration. The šadda -iyy final. ⁧شُرْطِيٌّ⁩ , ⁧صَحَفِيٌّ⁩ , ⁧جُنْدِيٌّ⁩ end up in ⁧ـيّ⁩ with šadda. Inside the sentence you can hear the double: šurṭiyyun ; pause becomes a ī long: šurṭī . To the female, the double always remains: ⁧شُرْطِيَّة⁩ šurṭiyya . The emphasis in the professions. ⁧طَالِب⁩ and ⁧طَبِيب⁩ begin with ṭāʾ: the tongue leans behind the teeth, the back retreats towards the throat and the ā the following darkens [ɑː]. In ⁧مُوَظَّف⁩ c'è ẓāʾ double, emphatic and dental: muwaẓẓaf . ⁧مِنَ⁩ + Article. mina l-Qāhira It's just one rhythmic unit: don't stop after min.
★ ⁧هُنَاكَ⁩ hunāka there ... adverb ...

Notes of use. ⁧مُوَظَّف⁩ indicates who works in an office, public or private: it is the word of the forms ('employees'). ⁧صَحَفِيّ⁩ read also ṣuḥufī : The two pronunciations are correct. ⁧شُرْطِيّ⁩ is the policeman in general; degrees and bodies you will see in the institutional vocabulary (A2). ⁧خَبَر⁩ also means "notice" (s): ⁧الأَخْبَار⁩ It's news, the news.
